newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Mandela - bad news for dictators.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mandela - bad news for dictators.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela has given a new impetus to African peace-making which diplomats and analysts believe could underpin the bruised continent's renaissance after decades of decline.
Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Tuesday confirmed that Mandela would soon host peace talks between him and President Mobutu Sese Seko aboard a South African navy ship.

Mandela's government has confirmed that the SAS Outeniqua, a second-hand Russian ice-breaker that is now the pride of the country's small navy, is already in international waters off the Zairean coastline in the Atlantic Ocean.
No date for the talks has been announced but South African Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister Aziz Pahad told reporters there was a possibility it could take place before the weekend.

Mobutu and Kabila's agreement for face-to-face talks is a diplomatic triumph for Mandela, the Nobel peace laureate who has tried throughout his three years as South Africa's first black president to share his vision of negotiated peace with his African neighbours.

"President Mandela is universally regarded as the most credible leader in Africa. He has been able to get the West involved in Africa's problems more successfully than anyone before him," said liberal Democratic Party leader Tony Leon.

"His involvement bolsters South Africa's prestige in the outside world and as long as we stick to moral diplomacy and don't try to get involved in physical peace-keeping, that's to everyone's benefit."
Mandela has made it clear that his calls upon the world's major powers are for support and not for leadership.

He told then U.S. secretary of state Warren Christopher on his final visit to Africa last year to think again about a U.S. proposal for an African crisis intervention force led, trained and financed by the West, but manned by Africans.
"Africa would like to feel that they are handling these things themselves...not acting in response to suggestions that come from outside the continent," he said.
A Western diplomat told Reuters that Mandela more than any other African leader had the moral authority to put a personal stamp on international peace-making efforts in the region.
But he said Mandela's integrity outweighed his experience.
"There is a growing interest in South Africa in trying to influence the foreign affairs of the region, but South Africa is very new to the game and the lack of experience shows.
"They bring the enormous prestige of President Mandela and only a modest capability to the problem," the diplomat said.

Mandela also has brought a level of personal integrity to the search for peace that makes it possible for him to break the mould of African solidarity and, sometimes, to state the obvious that others have not dared to acknowledge.
One such message from which he does not shy away is that Africa will never be a full player in the global economy while it is racked by civil wars and internecine conflicts.

"Mandela is forcing Africans to look differently at issues, to acknowledge the realities of the new world. He's bad news for dictators," said Vernon Seymour, an African analyst at the University of the Western Cape.
Mandela began the search for a peaceful solution to South Africa's own problems in a secret letter from his apartheid prison cell to then president P.W. Botha.

After 27 years in jail for plotting the end of white minority rule, he was freed in 1990 and led his guerrilla organisation into talks that ensured the dignified retirement and the legal absolution of apartheid's leaders and strategists and even its torturers.
That is what he has tried to do also for Zaire's Mobutu.

Aids said Mandela's pre-condition to Kabila for his support in the transition from 32 years of Mobutuism to democracy was that all parties in Zaire should be involved and that Mobutu's safety should be assured -- if necessary with asylum in South Africa.
"(Kabila) doesn't want a military solution...He wants a solution which receives the support of President Mobutu," Mandela told reporters recently.
"He has also made it clear that he has no intention of doing anything that would humiliate President Mobutu," he said.
Mandela's personal brand of inclusive peace characterises the search for a solution in Zaire, but the details come from his heir apparent, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki.
Another key member of Mandela's peace-making team is Pahad, the deputy foreign minister, who said in a recent interview:
"We can't avoid playing this role on the African continent of conflict prevention. There is a need for Africa to be better prepared to assist in African problems."

"We have always argued that if we had failed to play our role as a leading partner on the African continent Africa would begin to suspect that we had another agenda and so we had to play that role," he said.
